title: Matot: keep your word (Numbers 30:3)
hookLine: whatever a person vows, they shall do

lines: MATOT: THE HEADS OF THE TRIBES.
THE WORDS OUT OF OUR MOUTHS.
cards: I'll call you back. Let's get lunch sometime. I'll definitely be there.
These get said all the time, and some of them quietly evaporate. Nobody keeps score, mostly.
A new portion begins today, Matot, and it opens with Moses speaking not to the whole people but to the heads of the tribes, the leaders. The first subject he raises isn't war or land.
It's the words that come out of a person's mouth, and whether they mean anything.

teach.b: When a man makes a vow to the Lord, or swears an oath to bind himself, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, "he shall not break his word; he shall do according to all that proceedeth out of his mouth."
The word for vow is neder: a promise that binds you, often to give something, or to do or not do something. The Hebrew for break his word is lo yachel devaro.
Rashi links yachel to a root that means making something ordinary, profane.

Don't make your words common. Don't let them become cheap. The chapter goes on through cases: when a vow stands, and when, in that ancient household, a father or husband could cancel one on the day he heard it.
The Torah takes spoken words so seriously that it needs rules for undoing them. And because a vow is so binding, the later tradition grew cautious about making them at all.

teach.h: BETTER NOT TO VOW THAN TO BREAK IT.
teach.b: The book of Ecclesiastes says, in paraphrase, better not to vow than to vow and not pay.
Some Jews, when they promise something small, add two words: bli neder. Without a vow. I'll be there Thursday, bli neder.

It doesn't mean they don't intend to come. It means they know how heavy a real promise is, and won't make one lightly. And on the eve of Yom Kippur, the service opens with Kol Nidre, a formula about vows.
The Day of Atonement begins with the words people have said.

how: Some Jews add 'bli neder', without a vow, to everyday promises so that an ordinary intention isn't taken as a binding vow, and Yom Kippur eve opens with Kol Nidre, a formula concerning vows.

o: a gift set aside for the priests
a prayer of regret said before sleep
a vow: a promise that binds you

s: Matot opens with Moses speaking to the heads of the tribes
the first subject he raises is vows.
Jewish tradition encourages making as many vows as possible
it grew cautious: better not to vow than to vow and not pay.
saying bli neder means you don't intend to do it
it means you intend to, but won't make it a binding vow.

games.q: a friend asks you to help them move on Sunday. you mean to come, but you're not completely sure. what do you say?
games.why: some Jews would say bli neder: an honest intention, without turning it into a vow. words are taken that seriously.

practice: Look back over the last week for something you said you'd do, casually, and haven't done yet: a call, a text, returning something, an hour of help. Picture the person who heard you say it, and let your word feel solid again.

wordCard.voice: Neder. A vow, a binding promise. The Torah says: whoever vows shall not break his word, but do all that comes out of his mouth.

orig.note: Hebrew: a vow; the plural, nedarim, is also the name of a Talmud tractate about vows.

carryVoice: Your line: keep your word. Words aren't meant to be cheap. That's day four hundred seventy-one.
